title: Integrations
markdown:
External channels connect callers to the Executive. Each inbound adapter resolves the sender to a Person via `find_person_by_{slack,discord,telegram,email}_id` and threads `person_id` into `Executive.chat()`.

### Inbound channels

- **Slack** (`integrations.slack_bot`) — async Bolt socket-mode (`AsyncApp` + `AsyncSocketModeHandler`) embedded in the lifespan; responds to `@mention`s, DMs, and thread continuations.
- **Discord** (`integrations.discord_bot`) — discord.py gateway embedded in the lifespan; per-thread auto-titling, session-scoped memory, author attribution, configurable `@mention` thread promotion.
- **Telegram** — webhook gating + per-chat history.
- **Google Chat** — webhook + service-account auth.
- **Email** (`integrations.email_poller`) — MCP poll loop over the Executive's own mailbox — Gmail via `workspace-mcp` or Outlook via `ms-365-mcp-server`, chosen by `EMAIL_PROVIDER` (see *Workspace providers* below); never surfaces Reply-To redirects, filters auto-replies.

Slack, Discord, and Telegram are roster-gated on inbound: an unrostered sender's message is silently dropped (`details.outcome="rejected_unknown_sender"`). Email is not inbound-gated — non-roster mail flows through with a `[POLICY]` notice so triage can classify it. Slack/Discord thread continuations pass the shared `integrations.response_gate` (utility-fast model, biased toward replying).

### Attachments

`integrations.attachments` handles web chat, Discord, and Telegram. Images become Anthropic vision blocks; documents (PDF/DOCX/TXT/MD/CSV) are inlined into the turn that carried them and indexed into the ChromaDB `inbound_attachments` collection. 20 MB/file cap; web chat uses `POST /chat/upload`.

Indexed chunks are keyed on `attachment:<bare filename>` and tagged `type=attachment`. An attachment's name is chosen by whoever sent the message and the name is the chunk-id namespace, so without the prefix an inbound `strategy-2026.md` would upsert over the curated company document of that name. The prefix separates inbound content from curated uploads and keeps provenance visible; it does not separate senders from one another.

Isolation is the **collection**: `retriever.retrieve` never queries `inbound_attachments` at all, so an attachment cannot resurface as company knowledge in a later, unrelated turn. Attachment processing is roster-gated on Discord too — it previously ran before the gate, so an unrostered sender's file was downloaded and indexed before their message was dropped. These rows still have no operator surface: they are never written to `company/docs/`, so `GET /documents` does not list them.

This replaced a domain-based scheme that did not work. The chunks lived in `company_docs` under a domain outside the specialist set, on the premise that an unrecognised domain matched no filter. It matched every one — `ChromaDBStore.query` attaches a `where` clause only when a domain filter is present, and an Executive-level retrieval passes none — so attachments came back under “From your company documents”, top-ranked and indistinguishable from a curated upload. Legacy rows are migrated across on boot.

### MCP gateway & outbound

MCP runs in **both directions**. As a *client*, `orchestrator.mcp_gateway.MCPGateway` proxies MCP servers (Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Outlook mail and calendar — whatever `mcp_servers.json` configures) as Executive tools, with egress gating on Gmail recipients, Calendar attendees, Drive share grantees, and Microsoft 365 recipients/attendees against the roster (and a refusal of public / whole-domain Drive sharing). The Google Workspace server (`workspace-mcp`) behind those Gmail/Calendar/Drive tools runs **co-located inside the API** as a stdio child of the gateway — fitting the single-tenant model (one install = one company = one exec Google account), so there's no separate service to operate. It's baked into the API image and launched by `docker/workspace-mcp-launch.sh`, which selects single-user OAuth (token persisted at `/data/google_credentials`) or service-account domain-wide delegation from `GWORKSPACE_AUTH_MODE`. The gateway forwards the Google secrets to the child via `_FORWARDED_ENV_VARS`.

**Microsoft 365** is the Outlook twin: `@softeria/ms-365-mcp-server` (a Node package, pinned) is installed in a throwaway Node build stage and only the `node` binary plus the package are copied into the API image, launched by `docker/ms365-mcp-launch.sh` as the `microsoft_365` entry with an **explicit tool allow-list** (`--enabled-tools`, an anchored regex) rather than the upstream `mail,calendar` preset — that preset also registers inbox forwarding rules, mailbox settings (external auto-reply), calendar sharing and event forwarding, which can address people the gateway never sees. Exactly the Outlook mail + calendar tools are exposed (`microsoft_365__send-mail`, `microsoft_365__create-calendar-event`, …; hyphenated Graph endpoint aliases, proxied verbatim), and every admitted tool is either roster-gated or carries no recipient; the gate also covers the excluded writers in case an operator widens the list. Both servers can be configured at once. Auth is the MSAL device-code flow against the operator's own Entra app registration (`MS365_MCP_CLIENT_ID` is required; the server's built-in public client is refused); the refresh token persists at `/data/ms365_credentials` and is seeded once with `ms365-mcp-launch.sh --login` from inside the container — the server has a native device-code CLI, so there is no mint script and nothing to copy. The launcher scrubs the literal `$VAR` placeholders extensible-mcp leaves for unset variables (otherwise MSAL would be handed `$MS365_MCP_TENANT_ID` as an authority), and `MS365_MCP_EXPECTED_USERNAME` pins the bound mailbox. The egress gate for this family walks Graph's nested shapes (`body.Message.toRecipients[].emailAddress.address`, `body.attendees[]…`) — every email-shaped string outside the free-text fields must be on the roster, control characters and non-ASCII addresses are refused, unforeseen keys are still scanned (fail-closed) — and covers the whole write surface: send, reply, reply-all, forward, every draft tool, `update-mail-message` (it can PATCH recipients onto a draft) and create-/update-calendar-event; reads and `delete-calendar-event` (the only cancel path) pass through. Graph's reply, reply-all and send-draft actions carry no recipient in their arguments (the recipient is whoever the referenced `messageId` names), so for those the gate first reads the referenced message through the server and roster-checks the recipients Graph will derive (`replyTo` else `from`, plus the original to/cc for reply-all, the draft's own to/cc/bcc for send-draft), refusing on any lookup failure; RSVP and cancel actions get the same treatment through an event lookup, because their comment is emailed to the organizer or every attendee; `download-bytes` is pinned to mail attachment bytes only — which is what makes the poller's promise that an unrostered sender cannot be auto-replied to hold on Outlook as it does on Gmail; and the rendered inbound text quotes any forged `--- REPLY ---` line inside a body so the persona only ever reads the real block. Meanwhile `delete-mail-*`, `logout`, `remove-account` and `download-bytes-to-file` are denied by the example config's hyphenated patterns. A successful `send-mail` records the same outbound-context linkage Gmail does. As a *server*, `openexecutive.mcp_server` exposes OE's own company context and specialist council to external MCP clients at `/mcp` — the inverse direction; see the dedicated **MCP Server** section. The gateway launches extensible-mcp as a `uvx` subprocess whose fastembed tool-search index uses an embedding model baked into the API image and loaded offline, so it no longer re-downloads that model from the Hugging Face Hub on every cold start. Because the MCP stdio client does not inherit the parent environment, `MCPGateway.start()` explicitly forwards the embedding-cache/offline env vars (`FASTEMBED_CACHE_PATH`, `HF_HUB_OFFLINE`, …) into the child.

**Enablement, and why it degrades instead of dying.** `MCP_ENABLED` left unset is inferred from the presence of `mcp_servers_config_path` — dropping an `mcp_servers.json` next to `profile.yaml` turns MCP on with no further configuration. An **explicit** setting always wins in both directions: `MCP_ENABLED=false` keeps MCP off with the file still in place. It did not: `_resolve_mcp` tested `not self.mcp_enabled`, which cannot tell "never set" from "set to false", so the file's presence silently overrode the operator. The file is probed through `config.mcp_config_file_present`, never `Path.exists` directly — that re-raises an EACCES on a parent directory, and from inside a validator that comes out of `Settings()` itself, which `api/main.py` calls at module level. The check now reads `model_fields_set` (the fields the env actually supplied) and stores that on a private attr behind the read-only `mcp_auto_enabled` property, because the validator's own assignment joins that set and would otherwise make every auto-enable look explicit downstream.

Startup is **best-effort**, in `main._start_mcp_gateway`. Two checks come before the subprocess: MCP off is a no-op, and a config defining no servers under `mcpServers` is logged and skipped — extensible-mcp's own loader raises on that and exits, and because the child is already gone the only thing that surfaces is anyio's "Attempted to exit cancel scope in a different task" from `stdio_client` unwinding, a traceback naming nothing about configuration. The start is also bounded (120s, generous because that child may clone extensible-mcp on a cold start): `ClientSession` carries no `read_timeout_seconds`, so `initialize()` waits forever on a child that is *alive but silent*, and an unbounded wait is a lifespan that never yields — the same healthcheck-never-passes symptom, which no `except` can see. A gateway that fails anyway is logged at ERROR with the config path, the servers it named, and whether the config file or an explicit `MCP_ENABLED` turned MCP on, then torn down under its own timeout; the API boots **without MCP tools and without the email poller** rather than refusing to boot. The guard catches `BaseException`, not `Exception`, re-raising a bare `CancelledError` first: the original failure came from anyio, which wraps a task group's failures in `BaseExceptionGroup` as soon as one is a `BaseException` — and that group is not an `Exception`, so `except Exception` would miss the very shape this contains. The teardown is contained too, since it runs from inside that `except` and would otherwise replace the actionable log with the crash it prevents. `configured_server_names` never raises either, and deliberately catches broadly: it reads an operator-owned path during startup, where an exception is the crash loop rather than a bug report — `Path.is_file` re-raises an EACCES on a parent directory, and `json.loads` answers deeply-nested input with `RecursionError`, which is not a `ValueError`. It tests `is_file()` so a directory or a symlink to a FIFO is never opened, and caps the read at 1 MiB. That exception used to propagate out of the lifespan and kill the container — under `restart: unless-stopped`, a crash loop whose only outward symptom was a healthcheck that never passed. Outbound tools: per-Person DMs (`send_slack_dm`, `send_discord_dm`, `send_telegram_message`) plus room-targeted `send_department_message` and `send_company_broadcast`. The per-Person DMs are additionally rate-limited and de-duplicated by the outbound anti-spam guard (below).

### Outbound anti-spam guard

Every per-Person DM passes a deterministic guard (`orchestrator.outbound_guard.check_outbound_allowed`) after the roster gate and recipient-id recovery but before the network send — the single chokepoint **all** proactive DM paths reach (ad-hoc chat sends, the scheduler's followup/nudge dispatch, principal-brief delivery, the reflection turn, and research-finding routing). On a violation it returns a human-readable reason and the handler **suppresses** the send (`{"status":"suppressed","reason":…}`), writes a `tool_invocation` audit row with `suppressed=true`, and writes **no** `done` activity row — so a blocked attempt never counts toward its own rate cap, and the Executive can read the reason and hold or `schedule_followup` for the recipient's next window. Three controls: **content dedup** (a near-identical message — whitespace/case-normalized, first 160 chars — already sent to the same recipient within `OUTBOUND_DEDUP_WINDOW_MINUTES`, default 360); a **per-recipient rate cap** (`OUTBOUND_MAX_PER_RECIPIENT_PER_WINDOW`, default 5, over `OUTBOUND_RATE_WINDOW_MINUTES`, default 60); and **quiet hours / availability** (`OUTBOUND_RESPECT_QUIET_HOURS`, default on — refuse while the recipient is on leave or outside their `people.channel` availability windows, surfacing the next open window). Delivery history is read from the existing `status='done'` `scheduled_actions` rows (`episodic.recent_sends_for_channel_ref`), so there is no new table. The guard is **fail-open**: any internal lookup error returns "allow", so it can never turn a working send into a crash or a silently-dropped message. Principal briefs and the internal heartbeat kinds use the `__internal__` channel and never reach these handlers, so they are unaffected.

### Calendar & video links

The Executive books meetings through two typed tools over the configured calendar backend (`CALENDAR_PROVIDER`: Google Calendar via `manage_event`, or Outlook via `create-calendar-event` — see *Workspace providers*). `create_calendar_event` schedules a **future** meeting (propose→approve by default, or auto-execute once that decision class is promoted) and may be used proactively when a stalled goal warrants a sync. `create_instant_meeting` spins up an **impromptu call starting now**, auto-executing without the approval step and skipping the business-hours/horizon caps, so the Executive can hand back a join link immediately. Both attach a video-meeting link by default (`add_video_link`; opt out for in-person) — a **Google Meet** link parsed from the created event's `conferenceData`, or a **Microsoft Teams** link from `onlineMeeting.joinUrl` — surfaced to the caller plus persisted on the decision ledger as `meet_link`. The tool descriptions are static, backend-neutral text, so the cached tool block never depends on settings; the pre-rename `add_google_meet` key is still honoured for old ledger rows. Either way the caps that matter still hold — roster membership, principal-protection, max attendees, and a daily booking ceiling.

**Around-the-meeting participation.** The Executive doesn't join the call as a live voice; instead, on every successful booking it schedules a best-effort post-meeting follow-up (~5 min after the end) that DMs a human attendee asking for a quick recap — key decisions and action items. The reply flows back through the same cross-session DM context linkage described below, so the Executive can act on it (summarize, follow up) in a later turn. No meeting-transcript or Drive integration is required.

### Workspace providers

The Executive can *discover* any mail or calendar tool the gateway exposes, but three code paths call a fixed backend with no model in the loop and used to spell Gmail tool names inline: the inbound mailbox poller (list unread → fetch → mark read), alert email dispatch plus the scheduler's email send-tool hint, and the typed booking tools plus the approval-time conflict check. `integrations.workspace` puts those behind two Protocols (`MailProvider`, `CalendarProvider`) with one module per backend (`google.py`, `microsoft.py`) and a registry keyed on `EMAIL_PROVIDER` / `CALENDAR_PROVIDER` — separate switches (Outlook mail with a Google calendar is legitimate), both defaulting to `google`, so an existing install changes nothing until an operator opts in. The Google backend is the old inline code moved verbatim; tests pin its argument dicts byte-for-byte. The Microsoft backend polls only the Inbox folder (`list-mail-folder-messages` with `isRead eq false`, never the all-folders listing that includes Junk), converts Graph's HTML bodies to text with a real parser, marks read with `update-mail-message`, sends through `send-mail`'s nested shape, books with `isOnlineMeeting` + `onlineMeetingProvider=teamsForBusiness`, cancels with `delete-calendar-event`, and answers the advisory conflict check from the Executive's **own** calendar view (delegated permissions cannot read attendees' free/busy — narrower than Google's `query_freebusy`).

Every backend renders an inbound message into the same `Subject:` / `From:` / `To:` / `Cc:` + `--- BODY ---` text the persona already expects, followed by a `--- REPLY ---` block naming the exact reply tool and threading ids for *that* message (Gmail: `send_gmail_message` + `thread_id`; Outlook: `reply-mail-message` + `messageId`). The block rides in the user turn — which is what lets the cached persona say "use the reply tool in the REPLY block" instead of naming a vendor tool — and the scheduler's proactive-email trigger names the backend's send tool the same way. Providers never raise on a malformed backend response (they return empty / `None` / `{"error": …}`), so one bad cycle never kills a loop, and a chosen backend whose MCP server is missing from `mcp_servers.json` is logged at startup and skipped by the poller: fail-soft, never a boot failure.

### Cross-session DM context

When the principal says "DM Alex about X" in one session, OE sends the DM and — if a live conversation is active — records an `outbound_context` linkage row (recipient, full outbound text, originating session id). Email is covered too but recorded one layer deeper — there is no `send_email` tool, so the linkage is written in `orchestrator.mcp_gateway` after a successful `google_workspace__send_gmail_message` or `microsoft_365__send-mail`, one row per `to`/`cc` recipient keyed by the bare lowercased address (OE's own address skipped). When Alex later replies on the 1:1 DM path — or by email — the shared helper `integrations.inbound_hydration.hydrate_user_message` (called by the Discord, Telegram, and Slack handlers, and by the email poller keyed on the sender address) looks up the most-recent `open` linkage for that sender within 72h and prepends an `<outbound_reply_context>` block — the outbound text plus a backstory excerpt from the originating session — to the message handed to `Executive.chat()`. So OE knows what the reply is about instead of starting from an empty per-person session. The block lands in the user turn (caching rule) and is injected into a copy only — the pristine reply is persisted to history. The linkage is one-shot (consumed on first matched reply, race-safe) so an unrelated later DM isn't re-hydrated. This is deterministic and independent of the per-person `peer_memory` (Honcho) layer.
